purpose: Ceftazidime is an antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections in different parts of the body, such as the lungs, urinary tract, skin, blood, and brain. It is especially good at fighting a tough germ called Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Your doctor may use it in the hospital when other antibiotics might not work as well.
how_it_works: Think of bacteria as having a protective wall around them — without that wall, they fall apart and die. Ceftazidime works by blocking the bacteria from building and maintaining that protective wall. Once the wall breaks down, the bacteria cannot survive, and your infection clears up.
common_side_effects: Some people may notice redness, pain, or swelling at the injection site. You might also experience nausea, diarrhea, stomach upset, or a mild skin rash. Some people get a headache or a low-grade fever. These are usually mild and go away on their own.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you are allergic to penicillin or any other antibiotics, as you may also be allergic to this medication. Let your healthcare team know right away if you develop severe diarrhea, a serious skin rash, difficulty breathing, or swelling of the face or throat, as these can be signs of a serious reaction. This medicine can sometimes affect your kidneys, so your doctor may monitor your kidney function. If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or have seizures, make sure your doctor knows before starting this medication.
typical_dosing: Ceftazidime is given as an injection either into a vein (IV) or into a muscle (IM) — you will not take this one as a pill at home. The usual adult dose is 1 to 2 grams every 8 to 12 hours, but your doctor will adjust the dose based on the type and seriousness of your infection and how well your kidneys are working. Treatment usually lasts 5 to 14 days depending on your condition.
